raw_response:
I’m 59 this year, and I’ve farmed these fields long enough to know that stable production matters more than chasing the highest yield on paper. I have university training, so I do look at rates and timing more systematically than many neighbors, but with only 7 mu and some family members working off-farm, I still manage like a small household farmer: keep the wheat-maize rotation, control cash outflow, and avoid mistakes that would cost yield. This year I will stay with the full 7 mu in wheat followed by summer maize. For wheat, I’ll use a reliable improved variety, put most of the phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, split nitrogen between sowing and jointing, and irrigate mainly at overwintering recovery, jointing, and grain filling if rainfall is short. I’d rather not cut fertilizer too hard, because on my land the bigger risk is underfeeding the crop and losing yield. At the same time, I won’t overdo irrigation because well water costs money.

For maize, the key is the short turnaround after wheat harvest. I won’t waste time on heavy tillage. I’ll either direct-seed or do very light rotary preparation right after the wheat comes off, then get the maize in quickly to protect yield potential. I’ll use hybrid seed, apply base fertilizer with sowing, then topdress nitrogen around the big flare stage depending on rainfall and crop color. If summer rain is normal, one irrigation is enough; if it turns dry at tasseling, I’ll add another because that stage affects grain set too much to gamble. My main thinking this year is simple: keep the rotation steady, use moderate but adequate inputs, and protect yield with timely operations rather than spending heavily everywhere.
